steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that adapts the convex hull cheapest insertion heuristic to the traveling salesperson problem with precedence constraints (sequential ordering problem). Introduce the problem and its applications, explain why heuristics are used, describe the CHCI heuristic, and state our contribution and main result.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- TSP and TSP with precedence constraints (SOP): definition and applications
- Why heuristics, and the gap for TSP-PC
- The CHCI heuristic and why it works for the TSP
- Our contribution: the adapted CHCI (ACHCI) heuristic and its evaluation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) is, given a set of locations, to find the shortest possible tour that visits every location exactly once and then returns to the starting location. The TSP with Precedence Constraints (TSP-PC), also called the Sequential Ordering Problem (SOP), also has constraints that define precedence relations between the locations, and a tour is only feasible when the parent locations are visited before their children. These problems come up in many real-world applications where commodities need to be transported efficiently and there are precedence constraints related to picking up and dropping off items. Applications in the literature include freight transportation, crane scheduling in ports, job scheduling, automotive paint shops, helicopter scheduling and flexible manufacturing systems.

Heuristics that quickly find reasonably good solutions are usually used when TSP solutions have to be found instantaneously, or to initialize exact methods so they converge faster to the optimal solution. The reason is that exact methods for computing the optimal solution of TSPs are intractable, because the problems are \mathcal{NP} -hard. But effective heuristics for the TSP-PC have been neglected in the literature, and people commonly use the simple Nearest Neighbor (NN) greedy heuristic.

- CHCI
  - better TSP solutions than NN (NN used for simplicity)
  - convex hull subtour, then interior points inserted by increasing insertion cost
  - hull boundary points in same cyclic order as optimal tour
  - not adapted to TSP-PC: property fails with constraints
- Contribution
  - extend CHCI to TSP-PC -> ACHCI, expect lower cost than NN
  - initial tour: convex hull of pickup locations + starting position
  - insertions only into feasible segments; pickups anywhere, deliveries after their pickup
  - TSPLIB instances modified for spatial and precedence constraints
  - beats NN in 97% of cases when deliveries clustered around centroid

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) is, given a set of locations, to find the shortest possible tour that visits every location exactly once and then returns to the starting location. The TSP with Precedence Constraints (TSP-PC), also called the Sequential Ordering Problem (SOP), also has constraints that define precedence relations between the locations, and a tour is only feasible when the parent locations are visited before their children. These problems come up in many real-world applications where commodities need to be transported efficiently and there are precedence constraints related to picking up and dropping off items. Applications in the literature include freight transportation, crane scheduling in ports, job scheduling, automotive paint shops, helicopter scheduling and flexible manufacturing systems.

Heuristics that quickly find reasonably good solutions are usually used when TSP solutions have to be found instantaneously, or to initialize exact methods so they converge faster to the optimal solution. The reason is that exact methods for computing the optimal solution of TSPs are intractable, because the problems are \mathcal{NP} -hard. But effective heuristics for the TSP-PC have been neglected in the literature, and people commonly use the simple Nearest Neighbor (NN) greedy heuristic.

Among the heuristics, the Convex Hull Cheapest Insertion (CHCI) heuristic has been shown to give better TSP solutions than the NN heuristic, which is used a lot because it is simple. The CHCI heuristic starts with a subtour made from the convex hull of the points, and then the interior points are added to the subtour one by one in increasing order of insertion cost, until the tour is complete. Starting the candidate subtour with the convex hull of the TSP points helps to get good solutions, because the points on the boundary of the convex hull are visited in the same cyclic order as in the optimal TSP tour. However the CHCI heuristic has not been adapted to the TSP-PC, and there this property does not hold because of the added constraints.

The contribution of this paper is to extend the CHCI algorithm to the TSP-PC, since we expect it to reduce the tour cost compared to the NN heuristic. We call the proposed algorithm the adapted CHCI (ACHCI) heuristic. Its tours start from the convex hull boundary points of only the pickup locations and the starting position. For each insertion after that, the precedence constraints are kept by only allowing insertions into feasible segments of the subtour. So pickup locations can be added anywhere in the subtour, but delivery locations can only be added in the segment of the subtour that has already visited the matching pickup location. We describe the adapted approach with examples, and then we compare the reduction in tour cost against the NN heuristic, using TSPLIB benchmark instances that were reproducibly modified for spatial and precedence constraints. The experiments show that the algorithm does better than the NN heuristic in 97% of the cases when the delivery locations are clustered around the centroid of the point cloud made by all the locations of the TSP-PC.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Given a set of locations, the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) finds the shortest possible tour that visits each location exactly once and returns to the starting location. The TSP with Precedence Constraints (TSP-PC) [1], or Sequential Ordering Problem (SOP) [2], additionally has constraints defining precedence relations between locations, so that a tour is feasible only when parent locations are visited before their respective children. These problems arise in a variety of real-world applications where commodities must be efficiently transported while respecting precedence constraints related to picking up and dropping off items. Applications in the literature include freight transportation, crane scheduling in ports, job scheduling, automotive paint shops, helicopter scheduling and flexible manufacturing systems [3,4,5,6,7].

Heuristics that rapidly find reasonably good solutions are typically used when TSP solutions must be found instantaneously [8,9,10], or to initialize exact methods for faster convergence to the optimal solution [11,12], since exact methods for computing the optimal solution to TSPs are intractable due to their \mathcal{NP} -hard nature [13,14,15]. However, effective heuristics for the TSP-PC have been neglected in the literature [16,17], and the simple Nearest Neighbor (NN) greedy heuristic is commonly used [18,19,20,21,22].

Among heuristics, the Convex Hull Cheapest Insertion (CHCI) heuristic has been shown to produce better TSP solutions than the NN heuristic, which is frequently used because of its simplicity [23,24]. The CHCI heuristic starts from a subtour created from the convex hull of the points, and its interior points are then progressively added to the subtour in increasing order of insertion cost until the complete tour is obtained. Initiating the candidate subtour with the convex hull of the TSP points helps generate good solutions because points on the boundary of the convex hull are visited in the same cyclic order as in the optimal TSP tour [25,26,27]. However, the CHCI heuristic has not been adapted to the TSP-PC, where this property does not hold due to the added constraints.

The contribution of this paper is the extension of the CHCI algorithm to the TSP-PC, motivated by the expected reduction in tour cost compared to the NN heuristic. The proposed algorithm, referred to as the adapted CHCI (ACHCI) heuristic, initiates its tours using the convex hull boundary points of only the pickup locations and the starting position. For every subsequent insertion, precedence constraints are maintained by only permitting insertions into feasible segments of the subtour, which means that pickup locations can be added anywhere in the subtour, while delivery locations can only be added in the subtour segment that has already visited their corresponding pickup location. After describing the adapted approach with examples, we compare its reduction in tour cost to the NN heuristic using TSPLIB benchmark instances that have been reproducibly modified for spatial and precedence constraints [28]. This paper shows experimentally that the algorithm outperforms the NN heuristic in 97% of the cases when delivery locations are clustered around the centroid of the point cloud formed by all the locations of the TSP-PC.
